name: Iris Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on small building sites, mostly measuring boards, carrying materials, fixing trim, and doing the clearing nobody wants. I came into construction late and I'm still the junior hand at 58, which shows up in my pay. I like the moment a doorway finally fits, but the travel to the next site and wondering whether there is a next one wear me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little help with orders could save us standing around for missing screws. I used an AI phone tool once to turn a messy materials list into something readable, but I'd check every quantity myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Sam drives a school minibus part time, and my wage is the steadier one. We have less than a month's expenses saved, so an ordinary gap between sites worries me more than a clever ordering screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the current renovation and write the foreman a list of the trim sizes we repeatedly run out of. In the first year I'd keep using the phone tool for rough lists, check them against the tape measure, and put small leftovers into our rent envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy, mainly about what happens when this renovation finishes. A tool that catches a missing order would actually make my day easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check the phone's answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I compare every board length with my notebook before anyone places an order. Last month it rounded a doorway up, and that would have left us with the wrong trim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam about the rent envelope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Sam we're saving the odd twenty from a full week, not building a miracle fund. Our grown son and daughter have their own bills, so I want our rent to stay our job.

say: I'd say a **clearer materials list** could stop wasted site mornings.
I'd warn the foreman that every AI quantity needs a **tape-measure check**.
think: I worry more about the **gap between sites** than a modest tool.
I know Sam's **part-time minibus pay** would not cover our rent alone.
do: Keep working on the **current renovation** through its finish.
Check phone-generated lists against **measured trim sizes** before ordering.
Put spare wages from full weeks into the **rent envelope**.
feel: **Uneasy** about the next site, but pleased if orders improve.
S0.quote: Last month it rounded a doorway up, and that would have left us with the wrong trim.
fieldNote: Iris has tried a phone tool, yet uses her notebook and tape measure to keep **site errors** visible.
Her immediate worry is contract continuity, since her household has **under one month** of expenses saved.

steps.text: Keep working the current renovation through its finish
Check phone-generated materials lists against measured trim sizes
Put spare wages from full weeks into the rent envelope

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the desk in the site office will get smaller before the crew does. I'd also ask whether the new planning tools bring us materials on time or simply squeeze another room into Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office could run several jobs with fewer people, and that might mean more pressure on a junior hand who still makes slow cuts. Robots come slower here, but firms may stop hiring while they test them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the foreman to show me how the revised job schedule reaches my phone and practise checking it after work. In the first year I'd take the community centre's evening course in basic carpentry if the fee stays low, then apply for paid repair work when a site ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about being the slowest person on a faster site. I also know I learn a routine once somebody shows me why it matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the carpentry class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can fix trim, but my cuts still need a second look from the lead carpenter. A class with actual joints would help me earn the next contract, though I won't call myself qualified after six evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a tighter Friday look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The foreman might ask for two doorways instead of one before the last bus. I'd rather say a measured no than rush a cut and leave the next crew a crooked frame.

say: I'd say **site-office planning** will change before carrying and fitting do.
I'd ask whether faster schedules mean **better deliveries** or just harder Fridays.
think: I fear firms may **freeze hiring** while they test new equipment.
I worry a faster schedule will expose my **slow cuts**.
do: Practise checking the **job schedule** on my phone after work.
Take the community centre's **basic carpentry course** if its fee stays low.
Apply for paid **repair work** after this site ends.
feel: **Anxious** about pace, with some confidence in learning a useful routine.
S1.quote: I'd rather say a measured no than rush a cut and leave the next crew a crooked frame.
fieldNote: She connects software-led planning to a concrete question about **pace** on the building site.
Unlike a general promise to adapt, she names a particular **course** and says the fee must remain affordable.

steps.text: Practise checking the revised job schedule on the phone
Take the community centre basic carpentry course if the fee stays low
Apply for paid repair work when the current site ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the machine doing estimates in 2028 still cannot hang a door. I'd ask what happens to our site when robots that can hang one arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 60 at the thinking AI date and 63 at the robot date. If firms can buy hands that work without a wage, my junior place is exposed; neither Sam's minibus hours nor our savings could carry the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the foreman for a reference and collect photos of the trim I've fitted, with the owner's permission. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for building caretaker posts and keep taking construction shifts while they exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed, because three years after 2028 is a short path to losing my wage. I can make applications, but I can't make a vacancy appear in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which caretaker tasks could you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could patch trim and replace a broken latch; I'd need training on boilers and electrical faults. I wouldn't claim I can fix a system I've never opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no local post opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the minibus operator whether they need paid afternoon cleaning, then look along the next bus route for repair jobs. Moving house on our savings would be a bigger risk than travelling farther.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** does not yet fit doors on our site.
I'd ask the crew about the **2031 robot date** and the next contract.
think: I expect my **junior site place** could go once robots handle fitting.
I know our **thin cushion** cannot replace my wage for long.
do: Ask the foreman for a **reference** before the current job ends.
Photograph fitted **trim** with the owner's permission.
Apply for **caretaker posts** after 2028 while taking site shifts.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely wage loss around 2031.
S2.quote: I can make applications, but I can't make a vacancy appear in this town.
fieldNote: Iris understands that the greatest direct threat to her hands-on tasks comes at the **robot date**.
She gathers work evidence now, yet her plan remains constrained by **few local openings** and limited savings.

steps.text: Ask the foreman for a written work reference
Photograph fitted trim with the owner’s permission for applications
Apply for building caretaker posts after 2028
Keep taking paid construction shifts while available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a chance to see a machine on a real site before anyone tears up the rota. I'd ask the foreman for a demonstration, including the repairs after it breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when thinking AI arrives in 2031 and 66 when site robots arrive around 2034. I may be close to stopping heavy work. We can't set retirement by age alone when the rent still arrives monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking site work and enrol in the local hall's maintenance course if the council still runs it at a low fee. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for school caretaker and housing repair posts, then choose a paid offer over another unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, though five years lets me test a new route without walking out of this job. I can picture learning repairs more easily than starting from nothing at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from a robot demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see it fit an awkward old doorway, not a clean square one in a showroom. Those wonky frames are what make our days long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Sam stop working by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's minibus work may continue, but we shouldn't plan around it without asking the operator. I'd budget for both of us needing wages until we know otherwise.

say: I'd say a **real site demonstration** would tell me more than a promise.
I'd ask what happens when a robot meets a **crooked doorway**.
think: I may be **66** by the robot date, yet still need rent money.
I could use the warning to reach **paid maintenance work** before site hours shrink.
do: Enrol in the hall's **maintenance course** if the low-fee place remains.
Keep taking **site shifts** until a paid repair offer arrives.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to try another line of work in stages.
S3.quote: We can't set retirement by age alone when the rent still arrives monthly.
fieldNote: She asks for evidence from an awkward doorway because her own work involves **imperfect buildings**.
The five-year warning supports a specific low-cost course, but she prioritises **paid employment** over endless training.

steps.text: Enrol in the hall maintenance course if the low-fee place remains
Apply for school caretaker and housing repair posts after 2031
Keep taking paid site shifts until a repair offer arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to put a real plan on the calendar, if the work lasts that long. I'd want older workers shown the new equipment too, not quietly left off the training list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 68 when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and 71 when capable site robots arrive around 2039. I hope to be out of heavy construction by then, but a hope isn't the same as having rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the foreman to let me spend one paid morning with the maintenance crew when they finish this renovation. In the first year after 2036 I'd take lighter repair shifts if I'm still able, and seek local income advice before deciding whether I can stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier with that much warning, though my wages and health could change first. A decade gives us time to make smaller choices rather than one desperate jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those smaller choices be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I would keep the rent envelope and replace the leaking kitchen tap ourselves instead of paying a call-out. We'd review the bills each winter, because a long horizon can still disappear one short week at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does being left off training look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A younger hand gets shown the new saw, while I get sent to sweep. I'd ask to watch and practise safely, because I still need to earn while I'm here.

say: I'd say **ten years** gives us time to plan if the site work holds.
I'd ask that **older workers** receive equipment training too.
think: I hope to leave heavy work before **2039**, but rent may keep me employed.
I worry lost **training chances** could shorten my working years first.
do: Ask for one paid morning with the **maintenance crew** this year.
Take **lighter repair shifts** after 2036 if still able.
Seek local **income advice** before deciding to stop work.
feel: **Steadier** with time to adjust, though health and wages still worry me.
S4.quote: A younger hand gets shown the new saw, while I get sent to sweep.
fieldNote: Her ten-year plan is incremental and tied to present site access, rather than a promised **retirement date**.
She fears informal exclusion from **equipment training** could erode earnings before any capable robot arrives.

steps.text: Ask for one paid morning with the site maintenance crew this year
Take lighter paid repair shifts after 2036 if still able
Seek local income advice before deciding whether to stop working

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could reach my kind of work when I'm 63, while we're still paying rent from wages. A paid route into building maintenance and clear notice of site dates would help me act before the last shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether an older junior worker gets shown the useful new tools. If I'm only handed the broom, I'll have fewer chances to earn long before a robot can do my job.

headlineQuote: If I'm only handed the broom, I'll have fewer chances to earn long before a robot can do my job.
portrait: Iris is a **58-year-old junior** construction worker who fits trim and still wants to improve her cuts.
Her household has **less than one month** of expenses saved and depends mainly on her site wage.
She checks occasional AI help against measurements and seeks **paid maintenance work** as robot dates approach.
A longer warning gives her room for **low-cost training**, though she never assumes retirement is funded.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens her site income when capable robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid maintenance route** and clear site dates would let her apply before shifts disappear.
